hints: Start by thinking about what each method physically does - does it bring in a whole new piece of DNA from elsewhere, or does it cut and rewrite the organism's own DNA?
Remember that plasmid engineering adds a foreign gene, so it needs a donor of that gene. Gene editing can work by just changing or switching off an existing base or gene.
A tiny single base-pair swap from A-T to C-G, or knocking out one chosen gene, needs very precise targeting - which method is famous for that precision?
If only one or two bases are changed with no foreign DNA left behind, would a scientist be able to tell it apart from a spontaneous natural mutation?
Now decide row 1 - adding a completely new phenotypic characteristic like herbicide resistance or insulin production - can both methods do this, or only the older plasmid method?
walkthrough:
Picture the Two Methods Side by Side**
Think of plasmid engineering as delivery. You take a desired gene from a donor organism, put it into a plasmid vector, and transfer recombinant DNA into a recipient. That is why it must have a donor and a recipient, and why it is very good at adding a completely new trait that the organism did not have.

Picture Gene Editing as Precise Surgery**
Gene editing, such as CRISPR-Cas9, targets the organism's own genome. It can cut at a chosen sequence and either change a single base pair, for example A-T to C-G, or disrupt and inactivate a selected gene. No foreign gene needs to stay in the cell.

Apply to Each Row**
Both methods can give a new phenotype, so row 1 gets two ticks. Only editing can precisely rewrite A-T to C-G and knock out a chosen gene, so rows 2 and 3 are editing only. Because editing can leave only a tiny change with no vector DNA, it can look exactly like a natural mutation, so row 4 is editing only. Only the plasmid method needs a separate donor genome, so row 5 is plasmid only.

Final answer: Row 1 - add new phenotypic characteristic: tick both columns. Row 2 - change A-T to C-G: tick gene editing only. Row 3 - inactivate selected gene: tick gene editing only. Row 4 - indistinguishable from natural mutation: tick gene editing only. Row 5 - requires DNA donor and recipient: tick genetic engineering using a plasmid only.

hints: Look back at the text - wild type oil is high in polyunsaturated fatty acids which shortens storage. On Fig. 4.1, which type has the tallest bars for 18:2 and 18:3?
walkthrough:
Link Text to Bars**
Wild type is described as high in polyunsaturated fatty acids. In the key, 18:2 has two C=C double bonds and 18:3 has three, so they are polyunsaturated. Type A (black bars) shows about 25% 18:2 and about 18% 18:3, much higher than types B and C which are only about 3-8%. Type A also has low 18:1 at about 17%, while B and C have about 47% and 56%. So A matches the wild type description.
Final answer: A (type A is wild type).

hints: First describe the change in Fig. 4.1 - compare 18:1 in B and C with A, and 18:2 and 18:3 in B and C with A.
Link that shift from polyunsaturated to monounsaturated 18:1 to the longer storage time stated in the text.
Now think outward to people - if oil lasts longer and this crop grows in dry poor soils, what does that mean for waste, food supply, farmer income and where food can be grown?
walkthrough:
Read the Evidence in Fig. 4.1**
Type A has low 18:1 at about 17% and high polyunsaturates 18:2 and 18:3. Types B and C, the gene edited plants, reverse this: 18:1 rises to about 47% in B and about 56% in C, while 18:2 falls to about 3-4% and 18:3 falls to about 7-8%. That is a shift from polyunsaturated to monounsaturated oil.

Link Chemistry to Storage**
The text tells you high polyunsaturates shorten storage time. Fewer C=C double bonds means less oxidation and rancidity, so the edited oil stores for longer. Longer storage directly means less oil thrown away and more usable food from the same harvest.

Scale Up to Social Benefits**
Discuss means give the benefit plus the why. Longer-lasting oil plus a fast-growing crop that tolerates dry and poor soils helps food security in difficult regions, reduces shortages, provides stable income for growers and the local economy, and allows farming on land unsuitable for other food crops.

Final answer: Gene edited types B and C have more 18:1 (approx. 47% and 56% vs 17% in A) and less 18:2 and 18:3, giving longer storage. Social benefits: less food waste; more food production / fewer shortages helping meet global demand; more income for farmers / economic benefit; crop can be grown in dry poor soils / harsh environments where other crops fail.
